messages.content: I want to build a dependency-upgrade analyzer that distinguishes client-reachable behavioral incompatibilities from harmless upstream changes, even when dynamic dispatch and incomplete code make that distinction difficult.

The key distinction is whether a change can affect behavior the client can actually reach. An upstream difference alone does not establish a client-level incompatibility. At the same time, dynamic dispatch and incomplete code can make reachability or behavior uncertain, so the analyzer should not treat a lack of observed impact as proof that a change is harmless.
The evaluation target is at least 90% recall and 90% precision on 100 labeled upgrade scenarios.

That sets two separate targets on the same set of 100 labeled scenarios. Recall concerns how many labeled incompatibilities the analyzer detects; precision concerns how many of its incompatibility findings are correct. Both need to be at least 90%. The size of the set does not, by itself, say how many scenarios are incompatibilities.
I also need reproducible client-level witnesses for incompatibilities. What should that phrase mean here?

A witness should make the claimed incompatibility observable from the client’s perspective and be reproducible, rather than merely point to changed upstream code. Conceptually, it connects a client-reachable interaction to a behavioral difference associated with the upgrade. It supports the particular incompatibility being reported; it need not imply that every upstream change matters to that client.
So a changed upstream method is not enough on its own?

Right. The analyzer’s question is not simply whether upstream code changed. It is whether the change produces a behavioral incompatibility along a path reachable by the client. A change with no client-reachable behavioral effect can be harmless for this analysis, even though the upstream versions differ.
How should dynamic dispatch figure into that distinction?

Dynamic dispatch makes it harder to know which behavior a client call may invoke. The analyzer needs to account for that when assessing reachability: a call’s apparent form may not settle its eventual target. But dynamic dispatch is a difficulty to handle, not a reason to label every affected call incompatible or every uncertain call harmless.
And incomplete code means the analyzer may not be able to settle every path?

Yes. When relevant code is unavailable, the analyzer may be unable to establish whether a potential behavior is reachable or whether it changes for the client. That limitation should be identified explicitly as uncertainty caused by unavailable code, rather than presented as a confident finding of compatibility or incompatibility.
Reflection is another source of uncertainty I want called out explicitly.

Reflection can obscure which behavior a client may invoke, so it deserves an explicit uncertainty indication when it prevents a firm conclusion. The requirement is to identify uncertainty caused by reflection, just as it is to identify uncertainty caused by unavailable code. Neither source of uncertainty, by itself, demonstrates an incompatibility.
Does identifying uncertainty conflict with the precision and recall targets?

They are related but distinct requirements. The analyzer is meant to achieve at least 90% recall and 90% precision on the 100 labeled upgrade scenarios, while also being candid about conclusions it cannot establish because of unavailable code or reflection. The goal does not specify how uncertain cases are counted in that evaluation, so that counting should not be assumed here.
I want the reports to make clear why something is an incompatibility rather than just a suspicious upstream change.

For a reported incompatibility, the reproducible client-level witness serves that purpose: it ties the claim to behavior reachable by the client. A suspicious upstream change without such a connection remains different from an established client-reachable behavioral incompatibility. If the connection cannot be resolved because code is unavailable or reflection obscures it, the report should say so explicitly.
What about the word “harmless”? I do not want it to sound like a universal claim about the dependency.

Here, harmless is relative to the client-level distinction the analyzer is making. It means an upstream change does not amount to a client-reachable behavioral incompatibility in the scenario at issue; it does not claim that the change could never matter to any client. Nor should the analyzer call a change harmless merely because incomplete code prevents it from finding an effect.
So the analyzer has to separate a demonstrated impact, a change that is harmless for this client, and an impact it cannot determine?

That is a useful way to express the distinction without treating uncertainty as an answer. A demonstrated incompatibility needs a reproducible client-level witness. A harmless upstream change is one that does not yield a client-reachable behavioral incompatibility in the relevant scenario. Where unavailable code or reflection prevents that determination, the uncertainty should be explicit.
And none of the numerical targets says that this has already been achieved.

Correct. At least 90% recall and 90% precision on 100 labeled upgrade scenarios are targets for the analyzer, not reported results. The witness and uncertainty requirements describe what its incompatibility findings and unresolved cases need to convey.

I’m considering a combination of client-seeded points-to reachability and differential execution. The idea is to filter harmless upstream changes, replay incompatibilities, and flag reflection or missing code.

That is a proposal for dividing the problem into complementary parts. Client-seeded points-to reachability would focus attention on behavior the client might invoke, including possible targets of dynamic dispatch. Differential execution would then compare behavior across the upgrade for relevant client interactions. The intended outputs are to filter changes that do not amount to a client-level incompatibility, support replay of those that do, and make reflection or missing code visible as limitations.
What does “client-seeded” add to points-to reachability?

It keeps the reachability question anchored to the client rather than treating every upstream change as equally relevant. Points-to information can help account for possible dispatch targets, but its role here is to ask which changed behavior might be reached from the client. That is a scope for analysis, not yet proof of a behavioral incompatibility.
So a reachable change is a candidate, not automatically a finding?

Exactly. Reachability can establish a potential connection between a client interaction and changed upstream behavior. It does not, by itself, show that the two dependency versions behave incompatibly for that interaction. Differential execution is proposed as the complementary check on behavior.
Could you explain that complementary check without assuming it has already been built?

Conceptually, differential execution compares the client-level behavior associated with the versions on either side of the upgrade. If a relevant interaction shows an incompatible difference, replay can make the client-level claim reproducible. If the comparison does not show such a difference, that can help filter a candidate change rather than reporting every reachable upstream edit as an incompatibility. This describes the proposed use of execution, not an achieved result.
I want to be careful with “filter harmless changes.” Does that mean a run with no difference proves the change is harmless?

Not necessarily. An execution comparison speaks to the interactions it actually covers; absence of an observed difference should not be inflated into a universal claim about every possible client behavior. Here, filtering harmless changes means using the combined analysis to avoid incompatibility findings for upstream differences that do not produce a relevant client-level behavioral difference, while preserving uncertainty where the evidence cannot settle that question.
Then how do the two parts help with dynamic dispatch?

Client-seeded points-to reachability is the proposed way to consider possible targets behind a client call, rather than relying only on the call’s apparent target. Differential execution addresses a different question: whether behavior involving a relevant target differs across the upgrade. The combination is intended to reduce the gap between ‘this might be called’ and ‘this changes what the client experiences.’
And replay is specifically about incompatibilities, not just showing that upstream code changed?

Yes. In this proposal, replay is meant to support a client-level incompatibility claim: the relevant interaction should be repeatable so that the behavioral difference can be observed again. Merely showing a changed upstream location would not serve the same purpose.
What if the points-to analysis suggests a path, but the relevant code is missing?

The missing code should be flagged. A possible client path may remain, but unavailable code can prevent the analyzer from resolving what it does or whether it produces an incompatibility. The proposal calls for making that limitation explicit, not silently treating the candidate as either harmless or confirmed incompatible.
Would you handle reflection in the same spirit?

Yes. Reflection can obscure which behavior is invoked and therefore complicate the reachability assessment. Flagging reflection makes clear where the proposed reachability-and-execution combination may not support a firm conclusion. The flag communicates a limitation; it is not itself a replayable incompatibility.
Could a reflected call still have an observable behavioral difference?

In principle, a client interaction involving reflection could exhibit a difference. The point of flagging reflection is not to declare every such interaction unanalyzable or incompatible. It is to avoid presenting a confident reachability conclusion where reflection leaves relevant behavior unresolved.
I think the ordering matters conceptually: start from what the client may reach, then examine behavioral differences.

That captures the proposed combination. Client-seeded reachability narrows the relevance question; differential execution examines behavior for relevant interactions. The two ideas serve different purposes, and neither alone should turn every upstream difference into a client-reachable behavioral incompatibility.
Would the same distinction help explain why a changed dependency surface might not matter to this client?

Yes. An upstream change can exist without affecting behavior reachable by this client, and even a potentially reachable change need not produce an incompatible behavioral difference. The proposal uses client scope and behavioral comparison together to filter such changes, while keeping unresolved reachability or behavior visible rather than calling it harmless by default.
How would you describe the proposal in one sentence, without implying that the evaluation has been completed?

Combine client-seeded points-to reachability with differential execution to focus on client-relevant changes, filter harmless ones, replay client-level incompatibilities, and explicitly flag uncertainty from reflection or missing code.
How should client-seeded reachability handle reflective calls and missing library bodies without falsely dismissing reachable regressions?

It should distinguish “not shown to be reachable” from “shown to be unreachable.” A reflective call or a missing library body can interrupt the evidence needed to resolve a client path. When that happens, the analyzer should retain the possibility of a client-reachable regression and flag the source of uncertainty, rather than filtering the change as harmless merely because it cannot trace the path.
So the analysis can start from the client without pretending it knows every call target?

Yes. Client-seeded reachability defines the perspective: which library behavior might this client invoke? It does not guarantee that every target can be identified. If reflection obscures a target, the reachability conclusion should reflect that limit rather than silently treating the call as having no relevant target.
What is the corresponding issue with a missing library body?

A missing body may leave the analyzer unable to follow behavior beyond a known call or determine what that call can affect. The known portion of the client path still matters, but the absent portion cannot be used as evidence that no further relevant behavior is reachable. The uncertainty should be attributed to unavailable code.
Would it be fair to call every change beyond one of those gaps reachable?

That would go too far. A gap does not establish that every downstream change is reachable, just as it does not establish that none is. The important distinction is between a supported reachability conclusion and an unresolved possibility. Keeping that distinction explicit avoids both falsely dismissing regressions and treating every unknown as a confirmed client impact.
Then what is enough to filter an upstream change as harmless?

The filter should rely on evidence that the change does not create a client-reachable behavioral incompatibility in the case being assessed. Failure to find a path through unresolved reflection or missing code is weaker than that: it may only show that the available analysis could not complete the path. Such a gap should not, on its own, justify the harmless label.
Does differential execution resolve the uncertainty automatically?

No. Differential execution can reveal and help replay an incompatibility for a client interaction it exercises. But if a reflective target or behavior inside missing code remains unexplored, an execution with no observed difference does not automatically rule out a reachable regression there. Reachability limits and execution coverage should not be confused with proof of harmlessness.
If execution does show a difference, do I still need to mention reflection or the missing body?

A reproducible client-level difference can support the particular incompatibility it demonstrates. Reflection or unavailable code may still limit what the analysis can say about other paths or the completeness of its reachability assessment. A witness for one behavior should not be presented as resolving every uncertainty introduced by those gaps.
I want the output to distinguish a confirmed incompatibility from a suspected path through unavailable code.

That distinction is important. A confirmed incompatibility calls for a reproducible client-level witness. A path whose relevant behavior cannot be resolved because a library body is missing is an uncertainty, not the same finding. Likewise, a reflective call with unresolved targets should be identified as a reachability limitation rather than silently promoted to a demonstrated regression.
Could the analyzer still identify what it does know about a reflective call?

Yes. It can preserve any client-side path that is supported while saying precisely where reflection prevents a firmer conclusion about the invoked behavior. The point is not to erase the known path or to invent a target; it is to make the boundary of the available evidence clear.
And if the call reaches a library entry point but the body is absent?

It can distinguish the established connection to that entry point from the unresolved behavior beyond it. The missing body explains why the analysis cannot confidently classify the possible downstream effect. Reaching an entry point alone is not a client-level behavioral incompatibility, but the absent body is also not grounds for dismissing one.
This sounds like a question of what kind of negative conclusion the analysis is entitled to draw.

Exactly. “No relevant path was found” describes an analysis outcome; “no relevant path exists” is a stronger conclusion. Reflection and missing bodies can make the first true without establishing the second. To avoid falsely dismissing reachable regressions, the analyzer should keep that difference visible wherever those limitations matter.
Would explicit uncertainty undermine the goal of filtering harmless changes?

It places a necessary limit on the filter. The analyzer can still filter changes when it has sufficient grounds to treat them as harmless for the client. Explicit uncertainty prevents it from obtaining a cleaner-looking result by incorrectly labeling unresolved cases harmless. That is consistent with the aim of distinguishing client-reachable incompatibilities from upstream changes that do not affect the client.
So the safe formulation is not “reflection means incompatible,” but “reflection may prevent us from ruling an incompatibility out”?

Yes, when the reflective target remains unresolved and is relevant to the reachability question. The same reasoning applies to missing library bodies. Neither condition proves a regression; each can prevent a confident dismissal of one. A demonstrated incompatibility still needs client-level behavioral evidence, while unresolved cases should state what is unknown and why.

My hypothesis is that resolving reflection when its target is a constant string, then assigning unknown labels to unresolved reflective targets and missing library bodies, should reduce false-safe classifications compared with closed-world reachability.

That is a plausible hypothesis, not an established result. Constant-string reflection resolution could recover a target that would otherwise be hidden from reachability analysis. For cases it cannot resolve—and for missing bodies—an unknown label would keep the analyzer from treating an evidence gap as proof that a change is safe. The proposed comparison is specifically a reduction in false-safe classifications versus closed-world reachability.
What makes the constant string important?

If the reflective target is specified by a constant string, the analysis may be able to identify that target rather than leaving the call wholly unresolved. That can give client-seeded reachability a more specific path to consider. The hypothesis does not say that all reflective calls have constant targets or that resolving the target proves a behavioral incompatibility.
So reflection is not always just an unknown?

Right. The proposal distinguishes reflective calls whose targets can be resolved from those whose targets remain unresolved. It uses the information available in the constant-string case, while retaining an explicit unknown label when that information is insufficient.
What exactly would an unknown label assert?

It would assert a limit on the analysis: the relevant target or behavior has not been determined. It should not assert that a regression exists, and it should not assert that the change is harmless. Its purpose in this hypothesis is to prevent an unresolved reflective target or a missing library body from being mistaken for evidence of safety.
Why give missing bodies the same kind of label as unresolved reflective targets?

They create different gaps, but both can block a confident reachability or behavioral conclusion. An unresolved reflective call leaves the invoked target uncertain; a missing body leaves behavior beyond an available call boundary uncertain. An unknown label makes either limitation visible without pretending the two gaps reveal the same underlying behavior.
How does the closed-world comparison work conceptually?

In this comparison, closed-world reachability risks treating what it cannot see as though it cannot happen. If an unresolved reflective call or a missing body prevents it from tracing a possible client path, that can lead to a safe classification that the available evidence does not justify. Resolving constant-string targets where possible and marking the remaining gaps unknown should reduce that particular kind of false-safe classification. Whether it actually does so remains to be evaluated.
Does the hypothesis say the analyzer should classify every unknown case as incompatible instead?

No. That would replace one unsupported conclusion with another. Unknown means the evidence does not settle the case. The hypothesis is about avoiding false-safe classifications, not converting every unresolved target or missing body into a confirmed client-reachable regression.
Suppose a constant-string target can be identified. Is the case then resolved completely?

Not necessarily. Identifying a reflective target may help establish where the call could go, but reachability is not the same as showing an incompatible behavioral difference. Other limitations, including unavailable behavior, could still matter. Constant-string resolution addresses the target-identification gap only to the extent that the string actually determines a target the analysis can use.
And if the target cannot be resolved, I should not simply drop that call from the reachability picture?

That is the point of the unknown label for unresolved targets. Dropping the call as though it could not reach anything relevant could make a possible regression appear safe. Marking it unknown preserves the distinction between ‘no relevant target exists’ and ‘the target has not been established.’
How is a false-safe classification different from an ordinary uncertain result?

A false-safe classification says a case is safe when a reachable regression is in fact present. An uncertain result declines to make that safe claim because the available analysis cannot rule the regression out. The hypothesis predicts that explicit unknown labels, alongside constant-string resolution, should shift some cases away from unjustified safe classifications compared with closed-world reachability; it does not specify how many.
Would this approach still let the analyzer identify genuinely harmless upstream changes?

The hypothesis does not call for labeling all changes unknown. Where reachability and behavior can be assessed without an unresolved reflective target or missing body affecting the conclusion, the analyzer could still distinguish a harmless change. The unknown label is for a consequential gap in what can be determined, not a blanket label for every upgrade.
Could the comparison look better simply because the analyzer refuses to say anything definite?

That is a useful caution about interpreting the hypothesis. Reducing false-safe classifications alone would not show that every other classification is useful or correct. The claim here is narrower: compared with closed-world reachability, the combination should reduce cases incorrectly called safe because reflection or missing code was treated as absent. It is not a claim that uncertainty has been eliminated or that overall performance has already been demonstrated.
I also do not want ‘constant-string resolution’ to imply that reflection without a constant string is impossible to analyze in every circumstance.

Agreed. The hypothesis names one resolvable case: reflection with a constant-string target. It calls for unknown labels when targets remain unresolved. It does not assert that every non-constant reflective call must remain unresolved, or prescribe all possible ways a target might otherwise be determined.
Would the unknown label on a missing body say anything about which behavior that body contains?

No. It says the body is unavailable to the analysis and that a conclusion depending on it remains uncertain. It should not be read as a guess about what the body does, which client paths it ultimately permits, or whether it contains a regression.
Then the key comparison is not that this resolves every difficult call. It is that it should avoid calling an unresolved path safe just because the path is invisible under a closed-world view.

Exactly. The proposed improvement is selective resolution where a reflective target is given by a constant string, coupled with explicit unknown labels for unresolved targets and missing bodies. The hypothesis is that this combination should reduce false-safe classifications relative to closed-world reachability, while leaving genuinely unresolved cases identified as such rather than claiming they are confirmed regressions.

I want to turn this into a plan: implement constant-string reflection resolution, propagate unknowns through missing library bodies, replay differential witnesses, and compare false-safe rates against closed-world reachability.

Those four parts connect the reachability question to the behavioral check. Constant-string reflection resolution would make some reflective targets available to client-seeded reachability. Propagating unknowns through missing bodies would keep gaps in the available code visible. Replaying differential witnesses would support reproducible client-level incompatibility findings. Comparing false-safe rates with closed-world reachability would test whether the approach avoids incorrectly treating reachable regressions as safe. These are planned steps, not completed results.
What should implementing constant-string reflection resolution accomplish within reachability?

Where a reflective call’s target is specified by a constant string, it should let the analysis use that target when considering what the client may reach. The goal is to avoid losing a potentially relevant path solely because the call uses reflection. Resolving a target would not, by itself, establish that the target has an incompatible behavior.
I also want unknowns to propagate through missing bodies, not just appear as a note at the point where code disappears.

That matters because a conclusion may depend on what happens beyond the missing body. Propagating the unknown means preserving that limitation when assessing any conclusion that relies on the unavailable behavior. Otherwise, a path might appear to end at the gap, and a potentially reachable regression could be classified as safe without sufficient grounds.
Does propagation mean everything connected to a missing body becomes a confirmed incompatibility?

No. An unknown records that the available code does not settle the relevant question. Propagating it preserves uncertainty in conclusions that depend on the missing body; it does not turn every possible continuation into an established path or an observed behavioral regression.
How do the differential witnesses fit with that uncertainty?

Replaying a differential witness serves a different purpose: it supports a particular incompatibility by making the client-level behavioral difference reproducible. Unknown propagation marks what cannot be determined from the available code. A replayed witness can substantiate the behavior it demonstrates without implying that every uncertainty elsewhere has been resolved.
I would like the replay to say more than ‘some upstream change occurred.’

That follows from calling it a differential witness. Its role is to reproduce an incompatible difference at the client level across the upgrade, not merely to point to an edited upstream location. If a claim cannot be tied to such a replay, the plan should not present the upstream change alone as a witnessed client-level incompatibility.
Where does the closed-world comparison enter the plan?

It is the comparison for false-safe rates. The planned question is whether resolving constant-string reflective targets and preserving unknowns through missing bodies leads to fewer cases incorrectly classified as safe than closed-world reachability. The plan specifies the comparison, but it does not supply either rate or an outcome.
So comparing false-safe rates is not the same as assuming the proposed approach wins?
Correct. The comparison is an evaluation to perform. Its purpose is to determine how the rates differ; the plan itself does not establish that they do differ, or by how much.
What exactly makes a classification ‘false-safe’ in this context?

It is a safe classification that incorrectly dismisses a reachable regression. That is the error the planned comparison focuses on. An explicit unknown is different: it says the analysis lacks the basis for a firm safe or incompatible conclusion, rather than claiming a regression has been ruled out.
Could a resolved reflective target still lead into a missing library body?

Conceptually, yes. Identifying where a reflective call goes and knowing what happens beyond that point are distinct questions. The plan addresses both kinds of gap: resolve a target when the constant string permits it, and propagate uncertainty if missing code prevents a conclusion about the behavior that follows.
And if a reflective target is not resolved by the constant-string step?

The plan does not justify treating that call as harmless merely because this resolution step did not identify its target. The unresolved target remains a limitation to identify. Constant-string resolution covers the cases it can resolve; it is not a claim that all reflection becomes transparent.
Does the plan dictate exactly how unknowns are represented internally?

No. It calls for unknowns to propagate through missing bodies, which specifies how uncertainty must affect the analysis’s conclusions, but it does not prescribe an internal representation. The essential point is that a conclusion dependent on unavailable code should retain that uncertainty instead of quietly becoming a safe classification.
Nor does ‘replay differential witnesses’ specify a particular execution mechanism, right?

Right. It states what the replay should accomplish—make a claimed client-level behavioral incompatibility reproducible—without specifying an execution mechanism. The plan should not be read as evidence that such replay has already succeeded for any particular scenario.
I want the comparison to stay focused on false safety rather than folding every unknown into a success.

That is a useful distinction to preserve when making the planned comparison. An unknown avoids an unsupported safe claim, but it is not a confirmed incompatibility or a demonstrated harmless change. Comparing false-safe rates against closed-world reachability should keep those meanings separate, rather than treating uncertainty as proof that the analyzer has resolved the case.
How would you state the plan succinctly while keeping that distinction?

Implement constant-string reflection resolution and propagate unknowns through missing library bodies; replay differential witnesses for client-level incompatibilities; then compare false-safe rates against closed-world reachability. Unknowns would preserve unresolved cases, while replayed witnesses would support specific incompatibility claims. The comparison remains to be carried out.
I’m implementing ReflectionResolver for constant-string Class.forName/getMethod calls, and propagating UNKNOWN through missing library bodies in client-seeded call graphs.

Those are two related parts of the reachability work. ReflectionResolver addresses calls whose targets can be identified from constant strings. UNKNOWN propagation preserves the limits of a client-seeded call graph when a library body needed to follow a path is unavailable. Neither part, on its own, establishes a behavioral incompatibility.
What should ReflectionResolver contribute when it sees Class.forName with a constant string?

It should use the constant string to identify the class named by that reflective call, where the available information permits. That gives the call graph something more specific than an entirely unresolved reflective call. Identifying the class does not automatically settle every subsequent call or prove that a client-reachable regression exists.
And getMethod with a constant string?

The constant string can provide information about the method being requested. ReflectionResolver should use what that information actually determines, while leaving any remaining ambiguity unresolved. A known method name is useful for reachability, but it should not be stretched into certainty about behavior the available analysis cannot establish.
So the resolver should not make reflection look fully understood just because it found one string?

Right. Resolving a constant-string Class.forName or getMethod call means using the target information that can be established from that call. It does not mean every reflective target, possible invocation, or downstream behavior is known. Where the information stops, the reachability conclusion should stop too.
Why put that information into a client-seeded call graph rather than treating it as an isolated reflection finding?

The client-seeded graph asks what the client may reach. A reflective target matters to this activity because it can connect a client path to library behavior that would otherwise be obscured. Keeping it in that reachability context helps distinguish a potentially relevant target from a reflective call that has no established connection to the client.
The other part is propagating UNKNOWN through missing library bodies. What does propagation mean here?

It means the absence of a needed body remains visible in reachability conclusions that depend on what could happen through that body. The graph can retain the client path it knows up to the missing code, but it should not treat the unavailable portion as an empty path merely because its calls cannot be inspected.
Would UNKNOWN replace the whole known client path?

No. The established portion of the path and the unresolved portion convey different information. If the client can be traced to a call into a library body that is missing, the graph should preserve that supported connection while marking the continuation that depends on the body as UNKNOWN.
I want to avoid turning a missing body into an edge to everything.

That is consistent with using UNKNOWN. A missing body does not show that every possible target is reachable; it shows that the available call graph cannot determine the relevant continuation. Propagating UNKNOWN preserves that uncertainty without inventing specific targets or dismissing potential ones.
Does UNKNOWN mean there is definitely a regression behind the missing body?

No. UNKNOWN is a limit on what the client-seeded call graph can establish. It means the missing body prevents a firm conclusion where that body matters. It is neither a confirmed regression nor proof that the upgrade is harmless for the client.
How should I think about the interaction between ReflectionResolver and UNKNOWN?

They address different points where reachability can become unclear. ReflectionResolver can make a constant-string Class.forName/getMethod target more specific. If a path then depends on a missing library body, the target information does not make that body available; UNKNOWN still needs to propagate through the gap. Likewise, a missing body should not erase reflective target information that has been established.
Could a resolved reflective target still leave the client-seeded graph uncertain?

Yes. Resolving a target answers only the part of the reachability question supported by the constant string and available code. If the graph must pass through a missing library body, or if the reflective information does not determine everything relevant, uncertainty remains. Resolution should be as specific as the evidence allows, not broader.
What about reflective calls that ReflectionResolver cannot resolve from constant strings?

The implementation described here covers constant-string Class.forName/getMethod calls. A call outside what it can resolve should not be treated as unreachable merely because this resolver supplies no target. Its unresolved status needs to remain distinguishable from a supported conclusion that no relevant target exists.
I’m concerned that the call graph might appear complete when a library body is absent.

That is precisely the risk UNKNOWN propagation addresses. A graph may show a known path to a call while lacking the code needed to trace what follows. If a reachability conclusion depends on that continuation, carrying UNKNOWN prevents the displayed graph from implying that the path definitively ends there.
Does UNKNOWN have to propagate even when the missing body is irrelevant to a particular conclusion?

The important condition is dependence on the missing body. UNKNOWN should qualify conclusions whose reachability assessment relies on unavailable behavior. It need not erase conclusions supported entirely by available paths that do not depend on that gap. That keeps the uncertainty tied to what is actually missing.
Then the graph can have both a definite connection and an uncertain continuation?

Exactly. For example, it may be established that a client path reaches a particular library call, while the body of that call is unavailable. The first part is supported; what can be reached through the absent body remains UNKNOWN. Stating both is more accurate than declaring the entire path known or dismissing its continuation.
How does this activity help prevent false dismissal without declaring every change dangerous?

Constant-string resolution can recover client-relevant reflective connections that might otherwise be overlooked. UNKNOWN propagation prevents a missing body from being mistaken for evidence that no further relevant behavior can be reached. At the same time, neither a resolved connection nor an UNKNOWN gap is automatically an incompatible behavioral change; each conveys only what the reachability evidence supports.
I want the scope of this implementation to remain precise. Can you restate it without implying it is finished?

The activity is to implement ReflectionResolver for constant-string Class.forName/getMethod calls and to propagate UNKNOWN through missing library bodies in client-seeded call graphs. The intended effect is to represent resolvable reflective targets and preserve uncertainty where unavailable code interrupts reachability, without claiming that either step has already resolved all paths or established an incompatibility.
ReflectionResolver now emits client-seeded call graphs with resolved constant-string targets and UNKNOWN edges for unresolved reflection or absent library bodies.

That describes the artifact’s two kinds of information. The graphs record targets that ReflectionResolver can resolve from constant strings, while UNKNOWN edges mark places where reflection remains unresolved or a library body is absent. Because the graphs are client-seeded, both kinds of information are expressed in the context of paths from the client.
What should a reader understand from a resolved constant-string target in one of these graphs?

It means the available constant-string information identifies a target for the reflective call. That makes the target available to the client-seeded reachability picture. It does not, on its own, say that reaching that target changes client behavior across an upgrade.
And an UNKNOWN edge is not another name for a resolved target?

Correct. A resolved target conveys a specific connection supported by the available information. An UNKNOWN edge marks a connection whose relevant destination or continuation cannot be established from that information. The graph should not make those two kinds of edge look equivalent.
There are two stated reasons for UNKNOWN edges: unresolved reflection and absent bodies. Why preserve both?

They identify different limits. With unresolved reflection, the reflective target has not been determined. With an absent library body, the graph lacks code needed to establish what happens through that body. An UNKNOWN edge keeps either gap visible without asserting a concrete target or assuming the path simply stops.
If the graph has a known client path up to an absent body, does the UNKNOWN edge erase that known part?

No. The supported path up to the absent body remains useful information. The UNKNOWN edge identifies where the available graph cannot establish a continuation. A reader can therefore distinguish what is connected to the client from what remains unresolved beyond that point.
Could someone read an UNKNOWN edge as proof that the client reaches an incompatibility?

They should not. UNKNOWN describes a limit of the call graph, not an observed behavioral difference. It prevents an unsupported dismissal of a possible path, but it is not a reproducible client-level witness and does not confirm a regression.
Nor should the lack of a resolved target at an UNKNOWN edge be taken as proof of safety?

Right. If reflection is unresolved or a body is absent, the lack of a specific edge to a target may reflect missing information rather than the absence of a possible client path. The explicit UNKNOWN edge makes that distinction visible in the artifact.
Does the artifact say that every reflective call has been resolved?

No. It expressly includes UNKNOWN edges for unresolved reflection. It records constant-string targets that have been resolved and separately marks reflective connections that remain uncertain. Those are different outcomes within the emitted client-seeded graphs.
What if a constant-string target is resolved but the library body along the path is absent?

The two facts can coexist. The graph can retain the resolved target and still carry an UNKNOWN edge where an absent body prevents the continuation from being established. Knowing a target does not supply unavailable code or settle behavior beyond it.
I want to keep the claim about these graphs separate from the claim that an upgrade has been classified correctly.

That separation matters. This artifact describes what ReflectionResolver emits: client-seeded call graphs containing resolved constant-string targets and UNKNOWN edges for unresolved reflection or absent bodies. It does not, by itself, report a differential execution result, a replayed incompatibility, or measured classification accuracy.
So what does the graph actually let us say about a change connected to a resolved target?

It can support a reachability statement about the client and that target, to the extent represented by the graph. I worry that turning off fallback will make an incomplete path look definitively absent.

Would it help to describe the paths separately before comparing them?

Yes. State what the replay identifies with alias propagation, then what it identifies without alias propagation, and only then describe any difference. That keeps the evidence for each condition visible and prevents an UNKNOWN gap or an absent concrete path from being misreported as a confirmed negative finding.
Does the word ‘replay’ mean I already know which callback the residual case reaches?

Could disabling fallback make a condition appear more precise than it really is?

Is there a numerical outcome specified for this activity?

No. The activity specifies the residual ReflectionStress-20 case, the temporary disabling of UNKNOWN fallback, and the comparison with and without alias propagation. It reports neither a callback-path result nor a new false-safe or UNKNOWN count.

For ReflectionStress-20’s residual case, which concrete callback paths, if any, are identifiable with alias propagation and without it when UNKNOWN fallback is temporarily disabled? That question keeps the two conditions and the diagnostic setting explicit without assuming what the replay will reveal.

Can I say the replay identified the callback path?

Is the phrase “without it” potentially ambiguous?

Could I say the version without alias propagation failed to find a concrete callback path?

What is the narrow lesson about a missing concrete path?

Can the result tell us precisely where the alias appears in the callback route?

Should I describe alias propagation as sufficient to eliminate false-safe errors throughout ReflectionStress-20?

Include the condition: in this residual-case replay with UNKNOWN fallback disabled, alias propagation prevented the false-safe outcome by recovering the callback path. Without the condition, “necessary” could misleadingly imply that no other handling of uncertainty could avoid the error.

And does it show that the version without alias propagation is generally unsafe?

It shows one false-safe outcome for the residual case under the temporary fallback-disabled setting. It does not establish a general error rate for the version without alias propagation or say how it handles other cases.

With UNKNOWN fallback disabled for the residual ReflectionStress-20 case, ReflectionResolver recovered the callback path when alias propagation was enabled, but incorrectly classified the case as safe when alias propagation was disabled.
I’ve decided to retain alias-aware summaries for concrete callback paths and UNKNOWN fallback for unresolved ones. Both prevent different kinds of missed regressions.

That keeps two distinct protections in the analyzer. Alias-aware summaries preserve a concrete client-to-callback path when recognizing an alias makes that path identifiable. UNKNOWN fallback protects an unresolved path from being dismissed as safe merely because the analyzer cannot identify its callback target or continuation. They address different ways a reachable regression could be missed.
I don’t want UNKNOWN fallback to stand in for a concrete path when the alias-aware summary can actually recover one.

That distinction is central to the decision. When a concrete callback path can be supported, the analyzer should retain that specific reachability information. UNKNOWN is for a relevant connection that remains unresolved; it should not obscure a path the analysis can identify.
But I also don’t want an alias-aware summary to make an unresolved callback look fully understood.

Right. Accounting for an alias does not necessarily identify every callback target or settle behavior beyond unavailable code. Where a relevant part of the path remains unresolved, UNKNOWN fallback preserves that limitation instead of turning partial reachability information into an unjustified safe conclusion.
Can you clarify the different kinds of missed regressions the two parts are meant to prevent?

One kind arises when the analyzer loses a concrete callback path because it fails to connect references through an alias; alias-aware summaries retain that connection. Another arises when the analyzer treats a path it cannot resolve as though no relevant path exists; UNKNOWN fallback prevents that uncertainty from becoming an unsupported safe classification. The decision retains both rather than asking either to perform the other’s role.
Does an UNKNOWN outcome mean the analyzer has found the regression?

No. UNKNOWN says the available analysis cannot settle a relevant connection or consequence. It helps avoid missing a possible regression through a false declaration of safety, but it is not a confirmed incompatibility or a concrete callback path.
And a concrete callback path is not automatically a behavioral incompatibility either?

Correct. A concrete path supports a claim about what the client can reach. It does not, by itself, establish that the dependency upgrade changes client behavior incompatibly. Retaining the path makes the reachability account more informative without turning reachability into a behavioral witness.
Is the decision to choose whichever of the two produces fewer UNKNOWN labels?

No. The decision is to retain both capabilities for their different purposes. UNKNOWN labeling should reflect a genuine unresolved part of a relevant path, while alias-aware summaries should preserve concrete paths where they can be established. A lower label count alone would not justify dropping uncertainty that still matters.
How should they work together when only part of a client-to-callback route is concrete?

The analyzer can preserve the supported portion, including any alias-mediated connection it can establish, and leave the remaining relevant portion explicitly unresolved. That avoids two misleading extremes: presenting the whole route as concrete when it is not, or losing a supported connection because a later step is UNKNOWN.
I want the word ‘fallback’ to be understood carefully.

Here it means retaining an explicit unknown where the analysis cannot establish the relevant path, not inventing a callback target or declaring an incompatibility. It guards against treating incomplete reachability information as proof of safety.
Does retaining both mean every client call downstream of an omitted wrapper should be UNKNOWN?

No. The decision concerns concrete callback paths and paths that remain unresolved. UNKNOWN should qualify conclusions affected by a relevant unresolved connection, not automatically every downstream client call. Alias-aware summaries help keep identifiable connections specific; fallback preserves uncertainty where that specificity cannot be established.
Could I describe alias-aware summaries as replacing UNKNOWN fallback for alias-related calls?

That would be too broad. An alias-aware summary can recover a concrete connection when the evidence supports one, but an alias-related route may still contain an unresolved step. Retaining UNKNOWN fallback means such remaining uncertainty is not discarded simply because some alias information is available.
Does this decision claim that every reachable regression will now be detected?

No. It states which two safeguards to retain and why: they prevent different kinds of missed regressions. It does not claim complete reachability, resolution of all callbacks, or detection of every behavioral incompatibility.
Then the concise design statement is that concrete and unresolved paths need different treatment?

Yes. Retain alias-aware summaries to preserve concrete callback paths, and retain UNKNOWN fallback when a relevant path remains unresolved. Both matter because losing an identifiable path and falsely dismissing an unidentifiable one are different ways to miss a regression.

I’d like to synthesize minimized, version-pinned client tests for reachable changes. The tests would compare observable outcomes across the upgrade, while paths that cannot be tested would be reported as uncertain.

That proposal connects reachability to client-level behavioral evidence. A reachable change gives the analyzer a reason to investigate, but not yet a reason to call the upgrade incompatible. A version-pinned client test could make the comparison reproducible, while an untestable path would remain explicitly uncertain rather than being treated as harmless.
What does “client test” contribute that a report of changed library code would not?

It frames the comparison around an interaction available to the client. The relevant question is what the client can observe when that interaction is exercised against each dependency version, not merely whether the library’s code differs. A reported incompatibility would be stronger if the test reproduces the differing client-level outcomes.
I want to be precise about “reachable.” Does it mean every reachable change deserves a test that declares an incompatibility?

No. Reachability identifies a candidate for behavioral comparison. A reachable upstream change may leave the client’s observable outcome unchanged. The proposed test is meant to help distinguish those possibilities; reachability alone does not decide between them.
And “version-pinned” is about making the comparison repeatable?

Yes. The test should make clear which dependency version is used on each side of the comparison, so the observed outcomes can be reproduced under those versions. Pinning supports the witness’s reproducibility; it does not itself establish that the outcomes differ.
Would minimizing the test mean stripping away the client interaction that made the change relevant?

No. Minimization should retain what is needed to exercise the client-reachable behavior and, if there is a difference, reproduce it. Its purpose is to make the witness focused, not to remove the conditions that make the comparison meaningful. A smaller test that no longer reaches the behavior would not serve as a witness for that claim.
How should I think about the observable outcomes being compared?

They are what the client can observe from the test under each pinned version. The comparison should be stated at that level, rather than treating an internal upstream difference as a client-level result. The proposal does not prescribe a particular kind of observable outcome or say that every reachable change will produce one that differs.
If the outcomes differ, can the test immediately be called an incompatibility witness?

It can support that claim if the difference is an incompatible one for the client and the test reproducibly exercises the relevant client interaction under the two pinned versions. A difference alone should be described accurately; the proposal is about comparing observable outcomes to establish client-level incompatibilities, not assuming that every observable difference is incompatible.
What should a reader be able to learn from a successful witness?

They should be able to identify the client interaction being exercised, the pinned versions under comparison, and the incompatible difference in observable outcomes. Keeping the test minimized can make that connection easier to inspect. The witness supports that particular client-level claim, not a claim about every behavior of the dependency.
Could a minimized witness still leave uncertainty about other reachable changes?

Certainly. A witness establishes what its own test reproduces. It need not settle other paths, especially ones the analyzer cannot test. Reporting those paths as uncertain keeps the demonstrated incompatibility separate from questions that remain open.
What if a reachable path cannot be exercised as a client test?

Under the proposal, it should be reported as uncertain when it is untestable. The analyzer should not present the inability to execute that path as evidence that the upgrade is safe, nor invent an observable difference it has not reproduced. The report can preserve the reachable concern while being candid about the missing behavioral comparison.
Does “untestable” necessarily tell us why a path cannot be tested?

No. The proposal says to report untestable paths as uncertain; it does not specify a complete set of reasons a path might be untestable. Where reflection or unavailable code is what prevents a test or a firm conclusion, identifying that source of uncertainty would make the report more informative without claiming the path is incompatible.
Would you treat an unresolved reflective target as a test failure?

Not automatically. An unresolved target is a limit on what can be identified or exercised. If that limit makes a relevant path untestable, the appropriate report is uncertainty, with reflection identified as the reason where applicable. It should not be counted in the prose as a reproduced incompatibility or dismissed as harmless simply because no concrete test was produced.
And an unavailable library body can leave the same kind of gap?

It can leave a relevant part of the path or behavior unavailable for establishing a test and interpreting its outcome. If that prevents a reliable client-level comparison, the path should remain uncertain and the unavailable code should be identified as the limitation. The proposal does not assume that every missing body makes every nearby client interaction untestable.
Suppose a synthesized test runs on both versions and shows no differing observable outcome. What does that establish?

It establishes that this test did not show a differing observable outcome under the pinned versions. That can help filter an upstream change as a client-level incompatibility candidate for the interaction exercised. It does not, without further grounds, prove that no other client-reachable interaction can expose an incompatibility.
So the test should not turn a limited comparison into a universal declaration of harmlessness?

Exactly. Its evidential scope is the behavior it exercises. The proposal uses tests to compare observable client outcomes for reachable changes, while leaving untestable paths explicitly uncertain. Neither a test with no observed difference nor the absence of a test should silently settle paths outside the supported comparison.
Does test synthesis here prescribe how to generate inputs or minimize them?

No particular generation or minimization technique is specified. The proposed output is a minimized, version-pinned client test that exercises relevant behavior. How such a test is obtained is an implementation question; the proposal does not claim a method has been chosen or that synthesis will succeed for every reachable change.
Would the two pinned versions need to be compared using the same client interaction?

For the comparison to support a client-level behavioral claim, the outcomes need to be tied to a comparable client interaction on each side of the upgrade. Otherwise, a difference might reflect different tests rather than the dependency versions being compared. The proposal does not prescribe the mechanics of arranging that comparison.
What makes a witness reproducible rather than just an observation during one run?

The proposal’s version-pinned test should give someone a way to rerun the client interaction against the specified versions and observe the claimed difference again. Minimization should preserve the conditions needed for that repetition. The proposal does not assert that any such witness has already been synthesized or replayed.
Could the analyzer report a concrete witness for one path and uncertainty for another in the same upgrade?

Yes. Those reports answer different questions. The test could substantiate a particular client-reachable incompatibility, while an untestable path remains unresolved. A concrete witness for one path should not erase uncertainty on another, and an uncertain path should not undermine what the test actually reproduces.
Is the goal to write tests for all upstream changes, including ones with no connection to the client?

The proposal is scoped to reachable changes. Client reachability is what makes an upstream change relevant to the proposed test synthesis. It does not call for turning every upstream edit into a client test or treating unrelated library differences as incompatibility candidates.
What if reachability itself remains uncertain rather than established?

That uncertainty should remain visible. A concrete client test, if one can be synthesized and run, may provide evidence for the interaction it exercises. If the possible path cannot be resolved or tested, the analyzer should report the limit rather than present the absence of a witness as proof that the change is unreachable or harmless.
I want the reporting language to distinguish ‘no incompatible outcome observed’ from ‘the path could not be tested.’

Those should be separate statements. ‘No incompatible outcome observed’ describes the result of a particular comparison that was performed. ‘Could not be tested’ says the behavioral comparison was unavailable for a relevant path. Only the latter calls for the explicit untestable-path uncertainty in this proposal; neither should be silently converted into a broader compatibility guarantee.
How does this proposal relate to the requirement for client-level witnesses?

A minimized, version-pinned test that reproducibly shows an incompatible difference in client-observable outcomes could serve as such a witness. The proposal also accounts for cases where no test can be produced: those paths are reported as uncertain rather than assigned a witness they do not have.
Does proposing this establish any precision or recall result?

No. It proposes a way to compare reachable behavior and report uncertainty. It supplies no measured precision, recall, number of synthesized tests, or success rate for replay. Those outcomes would require evaluation; they are not consequences of proposing the approach.
Can you put the proposal in one careful sentence?

Synthesize minimized, version-pinned client tests for reachable changes to compare client-observable outcomes across the upgrade, and report paths that cannot be tested as uncertain rather than treating them as harmless or confirmed incompatible.
How can generated client tests reproduce changed behavior across both versions without treating nondeterministic output or missing code as an incompatibility?

The test needs to exercise a comparable client interaction under each version and compare what the client can observe. A differing output is only a candidate incompatibility: the comparison must distinguish a repeatable, version-associated behavioral difference from variation that can occur without changing versions. If missing code prevents the interaction or its outcome from being established, the appropriate conclusion is uncertainty, not an incompatibility finding.
What does it mean for the interaction to be comparable?

The client-level action being tested should remain the same in the two runs, with the dependency version being the difference of interest. Otherwise, a difference in observed outcomes might come from exercising different behavior rather than from the upgrade. Version pinning makes it clear which version produced each observation, but does not by itself make the observations comparable.
If the outputs differ once, should the generated test report a witness?

Not on that observation alone if the output could vary nondeterministically. A reproducible witness should demonstrate a difference that can be observed again under the stated comparison. One differing run does not establish whether the change is associated with the version or is part of ordinary variation.
Could repeating the test help separate those possibilities?

It could. Repeated runs under each pinned version can help reveal whether an apparent difference persists or whether similar variation occurs within a version. Repetition is a way to examine reproducibility, not a guarantee that every source of nondeterminism can be resolved.
What if both versions produce several different outputs?

Then comparing a single output from each version could be misleading. The question becomes whether there is a supported difference in client-observable behavior across the versions despite the within-version variation. If the observations cannot distinguish that from nondeterminism, the test should not be presented as a reproducible incompatibility witness.
Does a witness have to prove that every possible output differs?

No. A witness supports the particular client-level incompatibility it reproduces. It does need to make the claimed incompatible difference repeatable and attributable to the version comparison, rather than relying on an arbitrary choice among outcomes that either version might produce.
Could the test compare only the parts of an outcome relevant to client behavior?

Conceptually, yes, provided that doing so does not hide a difference relevant to the incompatibility claim. Comparing meaningful client-observable behavior can avoid mistaking irrelevant variation for incompatibility. The question does not prescribe a particular comparison rule, so any such rule would need to be clear about what it includes and excludes.
I do not want the analyzer to discard a real regression by calling every differing output nondeterministic.

That would be the opposite error. Nondeterminism is a reason to examine whether a difference is reproducible, not a blanket reason to ignore it. If the same client interaction consistently exposes an incompatible difference associated with the versions, variation elsewhere in the output should not automatically erase that evidence.
How does missing code differ from nondeterministic output?

With nondeterministic output, the test may execute and produce observations whose interpretation is uncertain. With missing code, the analyzer may lack the behavior needed to construct, execute, or assess the relevant client interaction at all. Both can limit a conclusion, but an unavailable body is not itself an observed difference between versions.
Suppose a test cannot reach the behavior because a library body is unavailable. Is that a failed incompatibility test?

It is an inability to establish the intended comparison, not a demonstration that the versions are compatible or incompatible. The relevant path can be reported as untestable or uncertain because code is unavailable. Calling the absence of a test result an incompatibility would invent a behavioral observation.
What if one version runs the test but the other cannot because code is missing from the analysis?

It matters why the second run cannot proceed. If code needed for the analysis or test is unavailable, that is a limitation on the comparison; it should not automatically be reported as changed client behavior. A demonstrated client-observable failure under an available, comparable run would be a different kind of evidence. The question does not give a particular case, so those situations should remain distinct.
Could an unresolved reflective call create the same problem?

Yes. If reflection leaves the invoked target unresolved, the analyzer may be unable to establish or exercise the intended client path. That should be identified as uncertainty caused by reflection, rather than treated as a successful test, a harmless change, or an observed incompatibility.
Does generating a test prove that the path is client-reachable?

A test that actually exercises the relevant client behavior can provide evidence for the path it exercises. Merely generating a test does not prove it reached the intended behavior. The claimed witness should connect the observed outcome to the client interaction and the change being assessed.
How does minimizing a test affect reproducibility when output can vary?

A minimized test still has to retain the client interaction and conditions necessary to reproduce the claimed difference. Making it smaller is not enough if removing context changes what it exercises or turns a repeatable comparison into an ambiguous one. Minimization and reproducibility have to be considered together.
Could pinning the two dependency versions alone control nondeterminism?

No. Pinning identifies the versions under comparison; it does not guarantee that either version produces an invariant output. A sound witness needs an observable difference that remains meaningful despite any variation relevant to the test.
I want a clear distinction between a comparison that finds no difference and one that cannot be performed.

A completed comparison with no incompatible outcome observed says something about the particular client interaction tested under the pinned versions. An unperformed or uninterpretable comparison gives no such observation. When missing code or unresolved reflection prevents the test, the report should say what blocks it and leave the relevant path uncertain.
Could a completed comparison with matching outcomes establish that the upstream change is harmless?

It can support that conclusion for the behavior the test actually exercises, but it does not by itself rule out a difference on every other client-reachable path. Matching outcomes on one test should not silently settle paths that were not exercised, especially ones that remain untestable.
What if the test runs, but its observations are too variable to decide whether the versions differ?

Then the outcome is unresolved on the available evidence. That differs from a path blocked by missing code: the test produced observations, but those observations do not support a reliable version-associated incompatibility claim. Neither situation warrants presenting a reproducible witness that the evidence does not provide.
Should the report give the same reason for both kinds of uncertainty?

No. It should distinguish uncertainty in interpreting variable observations from uncertainty caused by unavailable code or reflection. Saying why a conclusion remains open helps a reader avoid confusing a noisy completed comparison with a client path that could not be tested.
So what is the careful answer to the original question?

Use comparable, version-pinned client interactions and require a repeatable difference in relevant client-observable behavior before calling a generated test an incompatibility witness. Do not equate one variable output with a regression. If unavailable code or unresolved reflection prevents a meaningful comparison, report that path as uncertain rather than labeling it incompatible or harmless.
My plan is to generate minimized client harnesses, pin the dependency versions and seeds, replay the comparison five times, normalize observables, and mark paths involving missing code as uncertain.

That plan separates reproducibility from interpretation. The minimized harness keeps the comparison focused on a client interaction; pinned versions and seeds make the runs more repeatable; five replays provide repeated observations; and normalization helps compare the client-visible outcomes without treating incidental variation as a behavioral change. If missing code prevents a meaningful comparison of a path, the plan marks that path uncertain rather than calling it incompatible.
What does a minimized client harness need to retain?

It needs to retain the client interaction relevant to the reachable change and enough context to reproduce its observable outcome. Minimization is useful only if the harness still exercises the behavior under investigation. A smaller harness that no longer does so would not provide a client-level comparison.
Why pin both versions and seeds?

Pinning versions identifies the two sides of the upgrade being compared. Pinning seeds helps make seed-dependent variation repeatable, so an apparent difference is less likely to arise simply because the runs used different seed choices. Neither step alone guarantees deterministic behavior or proves that an observed difference is incompatible.
Should I say this plan eliminates nondeterminism?

No. Pinned seeds can control variation that depends on those seeds, but other variation may remain. The five replays and comparison of normalized observables are meant to help assess whether a difference is reproducible, not to assume that nondeterminism has disappeared.
Why specify five replays rather than just saying the harness is reproducible?

Five is the stated number of times to replay the comparison. It makes reproducibility something to examine through repeated observations instead of assuming it from a single run. The plan does not report the results of those five replays or say that five repetitions will settle every ambiguous outcome.
Does ‘replay five times’ mean a difference seen once in those five is enough for a witness?

The plan does not set that decision rule. A difference seen only once would need careful interpretation before being presented as a reproducible client-level incompatibility. The point of five replays is to observe how the comparison behaves repeatedly, not to make any one differing observation automatically conclusive.

Shared wall-clock reads make time input comparable; forcing equal callback sequences would suppress the scheduling behavior whose timing recall is being measured. Reproducibility should be assessed from the observed runs rather than imposed by making the two versions’ outputs match.
Could independent scheduling reduce false negatives but increase false positives?

It is possible in principle to expose more real timing differences while also seeing more variation on harmless cases. Measuring timing recall and false positives together is how the reruns can reveal that trade-off. No such change is reported yet.
Could it instead change neither measurement?

Yes. The modification is a proposed way to separate clock input from callback scheduling, not a guaranteed improvement. The activity requires the reruns to determine what happens on ClockShift-12 and UpgradeBench-100.
How does this differ from making both wall clocks independent?

Here the wall-clock reads are shared across the versions, preserving comparable time inputs. What is independent is callback scheduling. Making both time inputs independent would change the activity and make it harder to attribute some differences to the dependency version rather than clock variation.
Does a shared read mean every client-visible timestamp must be equal?

Not as stated. Comparable injected wall-clock reads do not require every output or timestamp produced by the versions to match. How each version uses the shared input remains behavior to compare. The activity does not set a rule that forces equal observable results.
Could a timing regression be visible as an outcome other than callback order?

Conceptually, yes, timing can affect client-observable behavior in different ways. This activity specifically changes callback scheduling and measures timing recall, but it does not enumerate the observables used for every scenario. Any claimed detection should remain tied to what the reruns actually observe.
What if a rerun is too variable for a definite timing verdict?

Then its instability should not be converted into a witnessed incompatibility or a verified harmless change. The measurement should reflect what can be supported by the observations and labels, rather than force a definite outcome solely to calculate recall or false positives.
Is there any result here about the two masked ClockShift-12 regressions?

Not yet. The activity is to make the WitnessHarness change and rerun ClockShift-12 and UpgradeBench-100. Whether either previously masked regression becomes detectable is among the questions the reruns can address, not a fact supplied by this activity.
Does this activity change how missing-code uncertainty is handled?

It does not specify such a change. The stated modification concerns shared wall-clock reads and independent callback scheduling, with timing recall and false positives measured on the two sets. No new missing-code uncertainty result follows from that description.
How should I summarize the work in progress without predicting success?

Modify WitnessHarness to give the versions shared wall-clock reads while letting them schedule callbacks independently, then rerun ClockShift-12 and UpgradeBench-100 to measure timing recall and false positives. The outcomes remain to be observed.
The reruns show that independent scheduling recovered all 5 ClockShift-12 timing regressions, and UpgradeBench-100 retained zero clock-driven false positives.

Those are results for two separate sets under the shared-wall-clock, independent-scheduling arrangement. All 5 ClockShift-12 timing regressions were recovered.
