Does “all 5” include the two timing regressions that were masked under the matched tick schedules?

Yes. Recovering all 5 ClockShift-12 timing regressions includes those two. The result does not give individual call sequences or witnesses for the cases, so the recovery should be stated at the reported count level.
Can I call that 100% timing recall on ClockShift-12?

For the five timing regressions reported on ClockShift-12, detecting all 5 corresponds to 100% recall within that category and set. Specify that scope; it is not an overall incompatibility-detection recall figure for every scenario.
What exactly does ‘retained zero clock-driven false positives’ mean?

It means the UpgradeBench-100 rerun reported no clock-driven false-positive incompatibility findings under this arrangement. It does not mean there were zero false positives of every kind or that all harmless cases received a verified harmless verdict.
Should I combine the results into a single accuracy percentage?

No. All 5 timing regressions recovered is a detection count on ClockShift-12; zero clock-driven false positives is an error count on UpgradeBench-100. They refer to different sets and different measurements, so combining them into one percentage would obscure what was actually observed.
Does this show that independent callback scheduling is always preferable?

It shows the reported outcomes for these reruns: recovery of all 5 ClockShift-12 timing regressions alongside zero clock-driven false positives on UpgradeBench-100. It does not establish how the arrangement behaves in every setting, or on error categories that were not reported.
Can I say the shared wall-clock reads no longer mask any ClockShift-12 timing regression?

For the five timing regressions counted in ClockShift-12, all five were recovered under the stated arrangement. That supports saying none of those five remained masked in this rerun. It does not rule out a different timing-sensitive case outside this set.
How much do we know about the five recovered regressions individually?
The result gives their count and category, not their individual interactions, schedules, or behavioral traces. Avoid adding case-specific explanations or assuming they all manifest in the same way.
Does the zero false-positive count tell us that scheduling introduced no extra variation?

No. It says no clock-driven false-positive findings were reported on UpgradeBench-100. The result does not describe all trace variation under independent scheduling or establish that the runs became deterministic in every respect.
What if someone says zero clock false positives proves the harmless-change verdicts are all correct?

That would overreach. Clock-driven false positives are one class of erroneous positive finding. The result does not report every harmless-change classification, every other false-positive cause, or how uncertain cases were handled.
Are these five recovered cases automatically stable five-run witnesses?

The evidence says they were recovered as timing regressions. It does not separately state that all five yielded stable five-run exported witnesses. Detection of a labeled regression and reproduction of a particular client-level witness should not be equated without that additional report.
Does the result include a new total witness-coverage count on UpgradeBench-100?
No. It reports zero clock-driven false positives there, not the number of labeled incompatibilities with stable witnesses. A coverage figure would need its own measurement.
Can I attribute the recovered regressions solely to the independent scheduler?

The result states that independent scheduling recovered all 5 ClockShift-12 timing regressions in the arrangement that also shares wall-clock reads. You can describe that observed association. The aggregate count does not isolate every implementation factor or explain the mechanism in each case.
Why is it important to mention the shared clock when describing the outcome?

Because the comparison’s point is to leave scheduling independent while retaining comparable wall-clock input. Saying only ‘independent scheduling’ could make it sound as though clock control was removed altogether. The reported zero clock-driven false positives on UpgradeBench-100 belongs to the arrangement in which wall-clock reads remained shared.
Does this settle the question of how to treat unstable traces?

No. These counts concern recovered timing regressions and clock-driven false positives. They do not report a new rule or outcome for every unstable trace. A difference that cannot be reproduced should still not be presented as a witnessed incompatibility on the strength of these aggregate figures.
Could another ClockShift-12 case be labeled harmless jitter and still get a false positive?

The evidence does not report outcomes for harmless-jitter cases on ClockShift-12. All 5 timing regressions being recovered does not tell us whether other scenarios in that set received erroneous positive findings.
What is the narrowest comparison the evidence supports?

With shared wall-clock reads and independent callback scheduling, the ClockShift-12 rerun recovered all 5 timing regressions, while the UpgradeBench-100 rerun had zero clock-driven false positives. Those observations address the two named checks without establishing every other classification outcome.
Can you put that in one concise report sentence?
With shared wall-clock reads and independent callback scheduling, all 5 ClockShift-12 timing regressions were recovered, and UpgradeBench-100 retained zero clock-driven false positives.
I’ve decided to adopt shared virtual wall-clock reads with independent callback schedulers. Synchronized ticks concealed regressions despite removing spurious clock differences.

That keeps the useful clock control while separating it from callback scheduling. Both versions receive shared virtual wall-clock readings, but neither version’s callback scheduler is forced to follow the other’s. The reason for that separation is important: synchronized ticks could remove spurious clock differences and still conceal genuine regressions.
Can you clarify what is shared and what remains independent?

The wall-clock readings supplied to the compared versions are shared. Callback scheduling remains independent for each version. Sharing a time input is not the same as requiring callbacks to execute in the same order or at corresponding points in the two runs.
So adopting a shared virtual wall clock does not mean synchronizing the event loops?

Correct. The decision explicitly avoids coupling callback scheduling to the shared clock readings. The versions can receive comparable wall-clock inputs while their callbacks follow their respective schedules. Otherwise the clock control could constrain the very behavior the comparison needs to observe.
Why isn’t removing spurious clock differences enough?

Because a comparison must also remain capable of showing a client-relevant regression. Synchronized ticks addressed spurious clock differences, but they concealed regressions. Eliminating an erroneous difference is valuable only if doing so does not also suppress a genuine behavioral difference.
Does this mean a shared wall-clock reading is considered harmless but a synchronized tick is not?

The distinction is about their effects on the comparison, not a blanket judgment that one kind of control is always harmless. The adopted arrangement shares virtual wall-clock reads while keeping callback schedulers independent. The stated reason for rejecting synchronization of callback scheduling is that synchronized ticks concealed regressions even as they removed spurious clock differences.
I don’t want independent schedulers to be interpreted as intentionally making the versions diverge.

They should not be. Independence means one scheduler is not forced to mirror the other. It leaves each version’s callback behavior available to observe; it does not direct the test to manufacture a difference or select a particular outcome.
Could the callbacks still happen in the same order under independent schedulers?

Yes. Independence does not require different outcomes. It means any matching order is observed rather than imposed by a cross-version scheduling control. Likewise, an observed ordering difference would need to be interpreted as client-relevant behavior, not treated as an incompatibility merely because the schedulers are independent.
How should we explain the role of the virtual clock without saying it determines the callback sequence?

Describe it as a shared source of wall-clock readings for the version comparison. Its purpose is to keep clock input comparable. Callback scheduling is a separate aspect of execution and remains independent, so the clock arrangement does not require the two versions’ callback sequences to match.
If sharing clock readings can still influence behavior, are the schedulers really independent?

They are independent in the sense specified by the decision: they are not synchronized to each other. Shared wall-clock input may still be relevant to how either version behaves. Independence does not mean callbacks are unaffected by time; it means comparable time input does not impose a shared callback schedule.
Is the problem with synchronized ticks that they created false positives?

No. The stated problem is that they concealed regressions despite removing spurious clock differences. The decision preserves the ability to avoid those spurious clock differences without accepting synchronization that hides client-relevant behavior.
Then the reason for retaining shared reads is distinct from the reason for independent scheduling?

Yes. Shared virtual wall-clock reads keep clock inputs comparable, addressing spurious differences caused by clock conditions. Independent callback schedulers avoid forcing callback behavior into alignment, which could conceal regressions. The decision combines those properties rather than treating clock control and scheduler synchronization as inseparable.
What would be an inaccurate summary of this decision?

Saying ‘make the versions execute identically’ would be inaccurate. The decision shares wall-clock reads, not all behavior. Saying ‘remove clock controls entirely’ would also be inaccurate: the shared virtual clock is retained. The point is to control the clock without synchronizing callbacks.
Does a mismatch between callback sequences automatically become a witnessed incompatibility under this arrangement?

No. Independent schedulers let a difference remain visible, but visibility is not a verdict. An incompatibility claim still requires evidence that the difference is reproducible, client-reachable, and behaviorally incompatible. The decision specifies the environment-control arrangement, not a rule that every scheduling difference is a regression.
And does a match between callback sequences establish that the upgrade is harmless?

Not by itself. A matching sequence in a particular comparison does not settle every potentially relevant client path or timing condition. The arrangement avoids imposing a match through synchronized scheduling, but an observed match still has only the scope of the behavior compared.
I want to preserve the causal wording about synchronized ticks. Can I say they concealed regressions even though they cleaned up the clock comparison?

Yes. That is the stated reason for the decision: synchronized ticks concealed regressions despite removing spurious clock differences. It captures why controlling an environmental input cannot be judged only by how many apparent differences it removes.
Does the decision require a particular implementation of the independent schedulers?

No particular scheduling mechanism is specified. The decision states the relationship: wall-clock reads are shared across versions, while callback scheduling is independent. It does not prescribe how schedulers are implemented or how individual callbacks are dispatched.
Does it require us to discard observations involving wall-clock values?

No. Sharing virtual wall-clock readings controls an input; it does not say to erase client-observable timing information. The reason for keeping callback scheduling independent is precisely to avoid hiding relevant behavior while removing spurious differences due to clock input.
Can the arrangement still leave a timing comparison uncertain?

Yes. Controlling wall-clock readings and leaving schedules independent do not guarantee that every client interaction yields a stable, interpretable result. Where the evidence does not settle a relevant behavior, uncertainty should remain distinct from both a witnessed incompatibility and a verified harmless change.
Should I present this as proof that no timing regression can ever be concealed again?

No. The decision addresses the identified problem with synchronized ticks by adopting shared virtual wall-clock reads and independent callback schedulers. It does not claim exhaustive coverage of every timing-sensitive interaction or eliminate every possible source of uncertainty.
What is the shortest statement that includes both the decision and its reason?
Adopt shared virtual wall-clock reads with independent callback schedulers: synchronized ticks removed spurious clock differences but also concealed regressions.
I propose introducing VerdictGate to combine reachability, reproducible differential witnesses, and explicit UNKNOWN labels, then measure verdict precision and recall on UpgradeBench-100.

VerdictGate would bring three kinds of evidence into one verdict decision: whether a change is relevant to a client-reachable path, whether a reproducible client-level comparison demonstrates an incompatible behavioral difference, and whether unresolved information requires an explicit UNKNOWN label. Measuring verdict precision and recall on UpgradeBench-100 would evaluate the resulting decisions. This is a proposal, not a reported implementation or result.
Why combine those signals rather than issue a verdict from reachability alone?

Reachability establishes that changed behavior might matter to the client; it does not establish that the client experiences an incompatibility. A reproducible differential witness addresses the behavioral question. UNKNOWN preserves a limitation when the available evidence cannot settle the relevant path or comparison. Treating any one of those as the whole answer would blur distinctions the proposed gate is meant to retain.
Does a reproducible differential witness make reachability redundant?

Not conceptually. The witness should be tied to a client interaction, while reachability explains why the changed behavior is relevant to that client. VerdictGate would combine those aspects rather than treat an upstream difference, however reproducible in isolation, as automatically client-reachable.
What should UNKNOWN contribute to the gate?

It should prevent an unresolved but relevant question from silently becoming a confident verdict. For example, if unavailable code or reflection leaves a consequential path unsettled, the gate can retain that uncertainty explicitly instead of equating an absent witness with a harmless change. UNKNOWN is not itself a witnessed incompatibility.
Could VerdictGate call something incompatible merely because the reachability graph contains an UNKNOWN edge?

That would overstate what UNKNOWN means. It marks a gap in what can be established, not an observed behavioral regression. The proposed gate should keep such a case distinguishable from one supported by a reproducible differential witness.
Conversely, could it call a change harmless whenever there is no witness?

Not on that basis alone. No witness might mean a comparison found no incompatible outcome for the behavior exercised, or it might mean a relevant path could not be resolved or tested. Combining reachability with explicit UNKNOWN labels is intended to keep those situations separate.
What would count as a reproducible differential witness in this proposal?

It would be a repeatable client-level comparison across the dependency versions that demonstrates an incompatible difference in what the client observes. Calling a comparison a witness should not rest solely on an upstream edit, a potentially reachable call, or a single uninterpretable difference. The proposal does not specify a new replay rule or claim that witnesses have already been produced for every finding.
If a concrete witness exists on one path but another path remains UNKNOWN, what does the gate do?

The witnessed incompatibility and the unresolved path have different evidential scopes. VerdictGate should not erase the witness merely because another path is uncertain, nor imply that the witness resolves that other path. The proposal does not specify a rule for compressing such mixed path-level information into a single upgrade-wide label, so that rule remains to be defined rather than assumed.
What about a tested path with no incompatible difference and a separate path blocked by missing code?

A completed comparison speaks to the tested path. It cannot by itself verify the path that depends on missing code. Combining the evidence should preserve the missing-code uncertainty rather than using the tested path’s outcome to declare the entire relevant behavior harmless.
Would explicit UNKNOWN labels need to say why a path is uncertain?

Yes, where the cause is known. An UNKNOWN attributed to unavailable code says something different from one attributed to unresolved reflection, and either differs from an unstable behavioral comparison. Naming the cause makes the limitation intelligible without guessing at the behavior beyond it.
Does VerdictGate determine whether reflection or missing code actually conceals a regression?

Not merely by receiving an UNKNOWN label. The label says the relevant question remains unsettled. VerdictGate can use it to avoid an unsupported dismissal, but neither reflection nor unavailable code proves that an incompatibility exists.
How should the gate handle a reachable change whose reproduced outcomes match?

Matching outcomes are evidence about the client interaction actually compared. Whether that is enough for a harmless verdict depends on whether relevant potentially affected behavior remains unexamined or UNKNOWN. The proposal names the evidence VerdictGate will combine but does not prescribe a complete harmlessness rule.
I want the verdict to be about the client, not about whether every upstream function changed.

That follows from combining client reachability with client-level differential witnesses. An upstream change with no supported client-level incompatible effect should not become an incompatibility finding just because it changed. Equally, uncertainty about whether the client can reach affected behavior should not be rewritten as a confident harmless conclusion.
Is VerdictGate supposed to replace the reachability analysis or the witness tests?

As proposed, it combines their outputs; it is not a claim that the gate itself discovers every reachable target or executes every client test. Its role is to make verdicts reflect what reachability, reproducible differential evidence, and explicit UNKNOWN labels jointly support.
What exactly would verdict precision measure on UpgradeBench-100?

Precision would concern how many positive incompatibility verdicts are correct against the benchmark labels, under a stated counting convention. The proposal does not give the counts, the label breakdown, or a rule for how UNKNOWN verdicts enter that calculation, so it cannot supply a precision value yet.
And verdict recall?

Recall would concern how many labeled incompatibilities receive positive incompatibility verdicts, again under a clear evaluation convention. A case left UNKNOWN is not a witnessed incompatibility; how such cases are counted and reported should be made explicit when measuring recall. The proposed evaluation has not produced a recall value.
Could simply labeling many difficult scenarios UNKNOWN make precision look better?

It might reduce the number of positive verdicts considered in a precision calculation, but that would not by itself show that labeled incompatibilities are being found. Measuring recall alongside precision, and reporting how UNKNOWN is treated, helps avoid mistaking selective abstention for complete analysis. No particular metric outcome follows from the proposal.
Should an UNKNOWN case be counted as a correct incompatibility because the gate avoided calling it safe?

No. Avoiding an unjustified harmless verdict is valuable, but UNKNOWN does not positively identify an incompatibility. The evaluation should distinguish uncertainty from a correct positive verdict rather than silently crediting the two as the same result.
Could the gate improve verdict precision while still having insufficient recall?

Conceptually, yes. Requiring strong witnesses could make positive findings more reliable while leaving some labeled incompatibilities without positive verdicts. The purpose of measuring both precision and recall on UpgradeBench-100 is to see how the proposed gate performs on each; neither can be inferred from the other.
Does this proposal report that the broader accuracy targets have been met?

No. It proposes VerdictGate and a precision-and-recall measurement on UpgradeBench-100. There are no verdict counts or new metric values in this node, so it would be premature to claim that an accuracy target has been achieved.
How should the results be reported if the gate produces incompatibility verdicts, harmless verdicts, and UNKNOWN labels?

The report should keep those outcomes distinguishable, state how each is compared with the benchmark labels, and give precision and recall using an explicit convention. It should not present UNKNOWN as a confirmed incompatibility or conflate a lack of witness with verified harmlessness. The proposal does not settle the exact reporting format.
What is the narrowest promise the proposal makes?

It proposes a place to combine reachability, reproducible differential witnesses, and explicit UNKNOWN labels into verdicts, followed by measurement of verdict precision and recall on UpgradeBench-100. It does not promise a particular classification for any scenario or a particular measured performance.
Can you state it succinctly without implying the gate has already been evaluated?

Introduce VerdictGate to make evidence-qualified verdicts from client reachability, reproducible differential witnesses, and explicit UNKNOWN labels, then measure its verdict precision and recall on UpgradeBench-100.
What VerdictGate criteria distinguish verified harmless changes from UNKNOWN paths when no differential witness reproduces?

The absence of a reproducing witness cannot make that distinction by itself. A verified harmless verdict would need affirmative grounds for saying the relevant change does not produce a client-reachable behavioral incompatibility within the scope being assessed. UNKNOWN is appropriate when a potentially relevant path or comparison remains unresolved. The question is what evidence VerdictGate should require for the first conclusion and what gaps prevent it.
So “no witness” is an observation shared by both possible verdicts?

Yes. It might mean the available comparisons found no incompatible effect on the relevant client behavior. It might instead mean a path could not be resolved, exercised, or interpreted well enough to produce a witness. Those circumstances support different conclusions, even though neither produced a reproducible differential witness.
Could a client-seeded reachability result establish that a change is harmless?

It can contribute to that assessment if it supplies a supported reason the changed behavior cannot affect the client. But a search that simply fails to find a path is weaker when reflection or unavailable code could conceal one. VerdictGate would need to distinguish supported exclusion of a relevant path from an incomplete reachability search before issuing a verified harmless verdict.
What if a potentially affected path is present but the client test shows no difference?

The test establishes what was observed for the interaction it exercised. Whether that supports a verified harmless verdict depends on whether it addresses the relevant client behavior and whether other potentially affected paths remain unsettled. A matching result for one interaction cannot settle a separate UNKNOWN path.
Would an UNKNOWN edge automatically make the entire upgrade UNKNOWN?

Not merely by existing. Its relevance to the verdict matters. If an unresolved edge could affect the behavior at issue, a harmless conclusion that depends on ruling it out would be unsupported. If a conclusion is independently supported and does not depend on that gap, the edge should not erase that evidence. The question does not prescribe how VerdictGate combines mixed path-level findings into one upgrade-wide verdict.
Can you explain what ‘affirmative grounds’ for harmlessness means without inventing a particular gate rule?

It means evidence bearing on the absence of a client-reachable incompatible effect, rather than only an absence of positive evidence. Conceptually, that could be supported reachability exclusion or a behavioral comparison sufficient for the particular client scope at issue. The question does not state a formal threshold or specify which combination of evidence VerdictGate must accept.
Suppose reflection prevents identifying a possible target. No differential witness reproduces. Which way should that lean?

If that unresolved reflective target matters to whether changed behavior can reach the client, a harmless verdict would be premature. The report should identify reflection as the cause of uncertainty, without claiming that the unknown target actually produces an incompatibility. A missing witness does not resolve the reflective call.
And if a library body is unavailable along the relevant path?

The unavailable body is likewise a reason to keep the affected conclusion uncertain when it prevents establishing what the client may reach or observe. It should not be interpreted as an empty body that proves harmlessness, or as evidence that an incompatibility has occurred. The cause can be reported explicitly as missing code.
Is UNKNOWN the right response to every incomplete library body anywhere in the dependency?

No. The question concerns paths relevant to the client-level verdict. Missing code elsewhere does not automatically defeat a conclusion that does not depend on it. The important question is whether the unavailable behavior could affect the change and client interaction being classified.
What if a differential comparison was run but its traces were unstable?

Then ‘no witness reproduces’ may reflect an inconclusive comparison rather than evidence of harmlessness. An unstable trace should not be promoted to a positive incompatibility finding, but it also cannot by itself verify that the change has no client-level effect. The report can identify instability as the limitation instead of attributing it to missing code or reflection without support.
Could matching normalized outcomes over the available tests be enough?

That depends on the scope those tests actually cover and whether their comparisons preserve relevant observable behavior. Matching outcomes support a negative finding for the interactions exercised. They do not automatically rule out other client-reachable paths, particularly paths that cannot be tested or whose targets remain unresolved.
Does calling a change ‘verified harmless’ require a claim about every other client that uses the dependency?

No. The verdict should be scoped to the client and upgrade scenario under assessment. ‘Verified harmless’ should not be read as a universal claim about the dependency. Even within that scope, it needs adequate support for the relevant client behavior rather than merely a failure to reproduce an incompatibility.
What if the gate has a concrete reachable path but no incompatible behavior in the observed runs, alongside an unresolved reflected path?

Those are different path-level outcomes. The observed runs provide evidence about the concrete path they exercised. If the reflected path could also expose the changed behavior and remains unresolved, those runs do not justify silently classifying that path as harmless. VerdictGate would need to preserve both the observation and the reflection-caused uncertainty when forming its conclusion.
And if a reproducible incompatibility is witnessed on another path?

The witness supports an incompatibility for the behavior it reproduces; lack of a witness on some other path does not negate it. Conversely, the witnessed path does not automatically resolve uncertainty about other paths. Your question about distinguishing harmless from UNKNOWN applies when no differential witness reproduces the relevant incompatibility claim.
Could an UNKNOWN label serve as a substitute for checking whether a change is harmless?

No. UNKNOWN is an honest description of a consequential gap, not a verification of either outcome. It prevents an unsupported safe conclusion, but it does not show that a tested, adequately assessed change is incompatible. The distinction should follow the evidence available for the particular client-relevant path.
I worry that an overly strict harmless criterion would make everything UNKNOWN.

That is a real design tension in the question. Requiring more evidence than the available analysis can ever provide could overuse UNKNOWN; accepting ‘no witness’ as sufficient would risk false-safe classifications. VerdictGate needs criteria that distinguish genuinely supported harmlessness from consequential uncertainty, rather than using either verdict as a default. The question itself does not establish that balance or a numerical threshold.
Could I say that a change is harmless whenever a reachable test completes without a diff?

That would be too broad without knowing what the test covered. It establishes no incompatible difference for that tested interaction under the observed conditions. It does not rule out a relevant untested route, an unresolved reflective target, a missing body, or an uninterpretable comparison. The harmless verdict needs evidence appropriate to the scope it claims.
Should VerdictGate identify a specific cause whenever it uses UNKNOWN?

It should state a cause when the evidence identifies one—for example, unresolved reflection, unavailable code, or an unstable comparison. It should not invent a more specific cause merely to make the verdict sound complete. Explaining the boundary of what is known is part of making UNKNOWN useful rather than a vague refusal to decide.
How do we avoid mistaking a harmless upstream edit for an incompatibility simply because reachability is UNKNOWN?

UNKNOWN does not assert an incompatibility. It says that an unresolved connection prevents a firm conclusion about the client-level effect. VerdictGate should reserve a positive incompatibility verdict for reproducible differential evidence, and reserve verified harmlessness for an adequately supported negative conclusion. An upstream edit alone, even beside an UNKNOWN path, proves neither.
Would the precision and recall measurement settle which harmlessness criterion to use?

It could show how a specified criterion performs against the UpgradeBench-100 labels, provided the evaluation clearly explains how UNKNOWN verdicts are treated. But no criterion or measured verdict counts are given in this question, so precision and recall cannot decide the issue in advance. The gate’s evidence requirements and the interpretation of its outcomes still need to be made explicit.
Can you state the core distinction without making it sound like VerdictGate has already implemented the answer?

The proposed distinction is evidential: no reproducing witness plus adequate support that the change cannot produce a client-reachable incompatibility could justify a scoped verified-harmless verdict; no reproducing witness plus a consequential unresolved path or uninterpretable comparison calls for UNKNOWN with its cause stated. Precisely what evidence qualifies as adequate support remains the open VerdictGate criteria question.
For VerdictGate, I plan to require closed client reachability and matched stable traces before issuing a harmless verdict. Unresolved edges or unstable replays should be classified UNKNOWN.

That gives a harmless verdict two affirmative requirements: the client-reachability assessment must be closed for the relevant change, and the compared traces must be stable and match. If a relevant edge remains unresolved or a replay is unstable, VerdictGate would use UNKNOWN rather than infer harmlessness from the absence of a reproducing differential witness. These are planned criteria, not implemented or evaluated results.
What should “closed client reachability” convey here?

It should convey that the reachability question needed for this client-level verdict has been settled, with no relevant unresolved edge left to conceal a possible effect of the change. It is not a claim that every path in the dependency or every other client has been analyzed. A graph that stops because a target or body cannot be determined would not provide that closure for a conclusion depending on it.
Does closed reachability mean the change must be unreachable from the client?

No. The client may reach the changed behavior, yet the compared client outcomes may still match. Closure concerns whether the relevant reachability assessment is resolved; matched stable traces supply the separate behavioral condition for the planned harmless verdict.
Why require the traces to match as well as be stable?

Stability and matching answer different questions. A stable trace is repeatable; matched traces show no difference in the compared observable behavior. Two versions could each produce stable traces that differ, so stability alone would not support a harmless verdict. Conversely, an apparent match in unstable traces would not provide the stable comparison the plan requires.
Does “matched” refer to the versions receiving comparable conditions or to their observed outcomes?

In the harmless-verdict criterion, it refers to the compared traces matching in the relevant observables. Comparable conditions are important to interpreting a comparison, but they do not guarantee matched outcomes. The plan requires stable observations that match, in addition to closed client reachability.
If no differential witness reproduces, can VerdictGate now just mark the change harmless?

No. The absence of a reproducing witness does not satisfy either affirmative condition on its own. Under this plan, the harmless verdict requires closed client reachability and matched stable traces. An unresolved edge or unstable replay instead leads to UNKNOWN for the affected conclusion.
How should an unresolved edge affect a test that otherwise has matching stable traces?

If the harmless conclusion depends on what lies beyond that edge, the matching test cannot close the gap. VerdictGate should classify the unresolved part UNKNOWN rather than use the tested interaction to declare the relevant change harmless. The supported observation from the test can still be reported for what it actually exercised.
Does any unresolved edge anywhere in a call graph have to make every verdict UNKNOWN?

The uncertainty should be tied to the conclusion it affects. An unrelated unresolved edge does not erase evidence about a path that can be assessed independently. But a harmless verdict should not claim closed client reachability while an unresolved edge relevant to that change remains on the path it needs to rule out.
What if reachability is closed, but a replay varies between runs?

Then the replay fails the stable-trace requirement. VerdictGate would classify that affected comparison UNKNOWN, not harmless merely because some observations happened to match and not incompatible merely because another observation differed.
And if replays are stable but the reachability assessment is not closed?

Stable observations establish something about the client interaction exercised, but they do not settle a relevant unresolved edge. The harmless verdict requires both conditions together. Where that edge could affect the conclusion, the planned classification is UNKNOWN.
Suppose the traces are stable but differ. Would this plan call the change harmless?

No. They would not meet the matched-trace condition. This plan specifies the criteria for harmlessness and when to use UNKNOWN for unresolved edges or unstable replays; it does not say that every stable difference is automatically a witnessed incompatibility. A positive verdict would need its own supported differential witness.
Should UNKNOWN tell the reader which requirement failed?

It should preserve the stated reason: an unresolved edge or an unstable replay, as applicable. Those are different limits on the conclusion. An unresolved edge leaves reachability open; an unstable replay leaves the behavioral comparison insufficiently repeatable. Neither should be mislabeled as a verified harmless outcome.
Can missing code or reflection explain an unresolved edge without changing the verdict rule?
